blocks.text:
#### Logging

Containers should write logs to standard output and standard error. The daemon's **logging driver** collects them. The default `json-file` driver stores one JSON object per line under the container directory and serves `docker logs`. Without rotation the file grows without bound, so `--log-opt max-size` and `max-file` are set per container or in `daemon.json`. Other drivers forward logs to syslog, journald, Fluentd or cloud services; with some drivers `docker logs` is unavailable. The `none` driver discards output.

### Worked example

All of the following were run on the build machine; the image `v2-base:1` provides bash and core utilities.

#### The writable layer and named volumes

blocks.code:
$ docker run --name v2-s1 v2-base:1 bash -c 'echo data > /tmp/note.txt; cat /tmp/note.txt'
data
$ docker rm v2-s1
$ docker run --rm v2-base:1 bash -c 'ls /tmp/note.txt 2>&1'
ls: cannot access '/tmp/note.txt': No such file or directory
blocks.title: Data in the writable layer is lost with the container

blocks.code:
$ docker volume create v2-vol
$ docker run --rm -v v2-vol:/data v2-base:1 bash -c 'echo persisted > /data/note.txt'
$ docker run --rm -v v2-vol:/data v2-base:1 cat /data/note.txt
persisted
$ docker volume inspect v2-vol --format 'driver={{.Driver}} mountpoint={{.Mountpoint}}'
driver=local mountpoint=/tmp/dk/data/volumes/v2-vol/_data
blocks.title: A named volume survives

blocks.text:
The mount point is inside the daemon's data root (here `/tmp/dk/data` instead of `/var/lib/docker`).

#### Bind mounts and ownership

blocks.code:
$ docker run --rm -v $W/host-dir:/mnt/shared v2-base:1 \
    bash -c 'cat /mnt/shared/h.txt; echo "written in container" > /mnt/shared/c.txt'
from host
$ cat $W/host-dir/c.txt; ls -l $W/host-dir | tail -2
written in container
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 21 Oct 20 03:12 c.txt
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 10 Oct 20 03:12 h.txt
blocks.title: Bind mount shares a host directory

blocks.text: Files created by the container process appear on the host owned by the container user (root here). A container that runs as an unprivileged user cannot write to a directory owned by root:

blocks.code:
$ docker run --rm --user 10001:10001 -v $W/host-dir:/mnt/shared v2-base:1 \
    bash -c 'id -u; touch /mnt/shared/new.txt'
10001
touch: cannot touch '/mnt/shared/new.txt': Permission denied
$ chown 10001:10001 $W/host-dir
$ docker run --rm --user 10001:10001 -v $W/host-dir:/mnt/shared v2-base:1 \
    bash -c 'touch /mnt/shared/new.txt && echo created'
created
$ ls -ln $W/host-dir | tail -3
-rw-r--r-- 1     0     0 21 Oct 20 03:12 c.txt
-rw-r--r-- 1     0     0 10 Oct 20 03:12 h.txt
-rw-r--r-- 1 10001 10001  0 Oct 20 03:12 new.txt
blocks.title: Permission error on a bind mount, and the fix

blocks.text: #### tmpfs

blocks.code:
$ docker run --rm --tmpfs /scratch:rw,size=8m v2-base:1 bash -c \
    'grep scratch /proc/mounts; dd if=/dev/zero of=/scratch/big bs=1M count=20 2>&1 | head -2'
tmpfs /scratch tmpfs rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,relatime,size=8192k 0 0
dd: error writing '/scratch/big': No space left on device
9+0 records in
blocks.title: tmpfs has a size limit and no persistence

blocks.text:
#### Backup and restore of a volume

A volume is backed up by mounting it read-only into a helper container together with a host directory and creating an archive (the helper image `v2-tools:1` contains tar and gzip):

blocks.code:
$ docker run --rm -v v2-vol:/data:ro -v $W:/backup v2-tools:1 \
    tar czf /backup/v2-vol.tar.gz -C /data .
$ ls -l $W/v2-vol.tar.gz | awk '{print $5, $9}'
155 /tmp/dvw_v2/bind/v2-vol.tar.gz
$ docker volume create v2-vol-restore
$ docker run --rm -v v2-vol-restore:/data -v $W:/backup:ro v2-tools:1 \
    tar xzf /backup/v2-vol.tar.gz -C /data
$ docker run --rm -v v2-vol-restore:/data v2-base:1 cat /data/note.txt
persisted
blocks.title: Volume backup and restore

blocks.text:
For a database, a logical backup with the database's own tool (`pg_dump`) is safer than copying files of a running server, which can yield an inconsistent copy.

#### Logs and rotation

blocks.code:
$ docker run -d --name v2-log --network none v2-base:1 bash -c \
    'for i in 1 2 3; do echo "line $i"; echo "err $i" >&2; done; sleep 30'
$ docker logs v2-log 2>/dev/null
line 1
line 2
line 3
$ docker logs --tail 2 -t v2-log 2>&1
2026-10-20T03:12:24.662140550Z err 2
2026-10-20T03:12:24.662142801Z err 3
$ head -2 $(docker inspect -f '{{.LogPath}}' v2-log)
{"log":"line 1\n","stream":"stdout","time":"2026-10-20T03:12:24.660997869Z"}
{"log":"err 1\n","stream":"stderr","time":"2026-10-20T03:12:24.661398825Z"}
blocks.title: docker logs and the json-file driver

blocks.text: The `2>/dev/null` hid the standard error lines; `docker logs` replays both streams. With `--log-opt max-size=10k` `--log-opt max-file=2` a container that wrote about 100 KB left two files of at most about 10 KB each in the container directory, for example `...-json.log` (730 bytes) and `...-json.log.1` (10052 bytes): the oldest data was discarded. With `--log-driver none` the log commands refuse to run:

blocks.code:
$ docker logs v2-log3
Error response from daemon: configured logging driver does not support reading
blocks.title: The none driver

blocks.text: #### Restart policies

blocks.code:
$ docker run -d --name v2-rs --restart on-failure:3 v2-base:1 bash -c 'echo run; exit 3'
$ docker inspect -f 'status={{.State.Status}} restarts={{.RestartCount}} \
    exit={{.State.ExitCode}}' v2-rs
status=exited restarts=3 exit=3
$ docker run -d --name v2-rs3 --restart unless-stopped v2-base:1 \
    bash -c 'echo started; sleep 1; exit 1'
$ docker inspect -f 'status={{.State.Status}} restarts={{.RestartCount}}' v2-rs3
status=running restarts=4
$ docker stop v2-rs3; docker inspect -f 'after stop: status={{.State.Status}}' v2-rs3
v2-rs3
after stop: status=exited
blocks.title: on-failure with a limit, and unless-stopped

blocks.text:
The first container was restarted three times and then left in `exited`. The second container looped (delays between restarts grow exponentially) until stopped manually, after which the policy no longer applied. The policy of a container can be changed with `docker update --restart`.

### Hands-on

Objective: prove that a volume outlives its container and practise backup.

1. Create a volume `lab-data` and run a container that writes a file into it, then remove the container.
2. Start a second container with the same volume and read the file.
3. Run a throwaway container that archives the volume to a host directory (`tar czf`), delete the volume with `docker` `volume rm lab-data`, recreate it and restore the archive.
4. Start a container with `--log-opt max-size=10k --log-opt max-file=2` that prints many lines and list the files at `docker inspect -f '{{.LogPath}}'`.
5. Run `docker run -d --restart on-failure:3 IMAGE sh -c 'exit 1'` and check `RestartCount` after a few seconds.

Expected result: the file survives step 1, the restore reproduces it, at most two log files exist and the restart count stops at 3.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 13: data lost after the container was removed

**Scenario.** A PostgreSQL container is recreated with a new image version and the tables are gone.

**Symptoms.** The database starts empty; `docker volume ls` shows a different anonymous volume or none.

**Diagnosis.** `docker inspect NAME --format '{{json .Mounts}}'` shows whether the data directory is a named volume, a bind mount or part of the writable layer. The demonstration with Compose confirmed the rule: after `docker` `compose down` the named volume `pgdata` remained and the table still contained 2 rows after the next `up`; after `docker` `compose down -v` the volume was deleted and the next start reported `relation "orders" does not exist`.

**Root cause.** Data written to the writable layer, or to an anonymous volume that was not reused, does not survive recreation. The option `-v` of `docker compose down` also deletes named volumes.

**Fix.** Mount a named volume (or a bind mount) on the data directory, and reuse it on recreation. Restore from backup if the volume was deleted.

**Prevention.** Declare the volume in Compose or the run command, never use `down -v` against environments with data, and take regular logical backups.

#### Problem 14: permission denied on a bind-mounted directory

**Scenario.** The application runs as UID 10001 and writes uploads to `/data`, bind-mounted from the host.

**Symptoms.** `Permission denied` or `AccessDeniedException` when writing; reads work.

**Diagnosis.** Compare `id -u` inside the container with `ls -ln` of the directory (see the experiment above: UID 10001 was denied on a root-owned directory).

**Root cause.** A bind mount keeps host ownership and mode. The container user's numeric UID does not match the owner.

**Fix.** `chown` the host directory to the container UID, run the container with `--user` equal to the directory owner, or use a named volume, which is initialised from the image directory ownership.

**Prevention.** Use numeric UIDs consistently and document the ownership requirement. On SELinux hosts, volume options such as `:z` are additionally needed (from memory, verify).

#### Problem 15: disk full from images, volumes and logs

**Scenario.** A build server or host becomes read-only because `/var/lib/docker` fills up.

**Symptoms.** `no space left on device` from builds or database writes.

**Diagnosis.** `docker system df` summarises usage by type. Output from the build machine (the daemon contained only the images of this Part and a few unused volumes):

blocks.code:
$ docker system df
TYPE            TOTAL     ACTIVE    SIZE      RECLAIMABLE
Images          17        0         1.147GB   77.26MB (6%)
Containers      0         0         0B        0B
Local Volumes   2         0         47.7MB    47.7MB (100%)
Build Cache     119       0         1.226GB   70.82MB
blocks.title: Disk usage by object type

blocks.text:
`du -sh /var/lib/docker/containers/*` shows oversized `*-json.log` files.

**Root cause.** Old image versions accumulate with each release, build cache grows, unused volumes remain, and json-file logs without rotation grow until the disk is full.

**Fix.** Remove what is verified as unused: `docker image prune`, `docker builder prune --filter until=168h`, `docker` `volume ls -f dangling=true` before `docker volume rm`. Avoid `docker system prune --volumes` on hosts with data, because it can delete volumes of stopped containers. Set log rotation in `/etc/docker/daemon.json`: `{"log-driver":` `"json-file", "log-opts": {"max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3"}}`.

**Prevention.** Scheduled pruning of images and cache with an age filter, log rotation by default and an alert on disk usage.

### Questions to expect

**Q1. What is the difference between** `docker stop` **and** `docker kill`**?** `stop` sends SIGTERM and, after a timeout (10 s by default), SIGKILL; `kill` sends SIGKILL (or a chosen signal) immediately. Only `stop` allows a graceful shutdown.

**Q2. Where does container data go and what survives removal?** Writes go to the writable overlay layer, deleted with the container. Named volumes and bind mounts persist; tmpfs data does not.

**Q3. Volume or bind mount?** Volumes are managed by Docker, portable between hosts' directory layouts and preferred for production data. Bind mounts expose a specific host path and suit development and configuration files.

**Q4. What restart policies exist?** `no`, `on-failure[:max]`, `always` and `unless-stopped`. They apply only after the container started successfully and do not repair the cause of a crash.

**Q5. How should an application log in a container?** To standard output and error, one event per line, leaving collection to the logging driver or the platform; the log file inside the container is avoided.

**Q6. How are logs rotated?** With the `json-file` options `max-size` and `max-file`, per container or in `daemon.json`. Without them the file grows without bound.

**Q7. How is a volume backed up?** A helper container mounts the volume (read-only) and a host directory and creates a tar archive; for databases the native dump tool is preferred.

**Q8. What does** `docker exec` **do?** It starts an extra process in the namespaces and cgroup of a running container; it does not start a new container.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A container's writable layer dies with it; persistent data needs a volume or bind mount.
- Run containers with explicit names, restart policies and log rotation; monitor RestartCount.
- Bind mounts inherit host ownership; align UIDs or use volumes.
- stop is graceful (SIGTERM then SIGKILL), kill is immediate.
- Use docker system df and targeted prune commands to keep disks healthy; never prune volumes blindly.

Containers must talk to each other and to the outside world, yet each has its own network namespace with its own interfaces and loopback address. A service such as `orders-service` must find the database without hard-coded IP addresses, which change on every start. Docker provides several network drivers and an embedded DNS server for this purpose. This chapter explains the models, what happens when a port is published and the single mistake that causes most connectivity failures: using `localhost` for another container.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Network modes

rows: A virtual switch per network; containers get private addresses and can resolve each other by name
The legacy default network; no name resolution between containers
The container shares the host network stack; no isolation, no port mapping
Joins the network namespace of another container

blocks.text:
#### Service discovery by DNS

In a user-defined bridge network the daemon runs an embedded DNS server, reachable at `127.0.0.11` from inside every container. It answers queries for container names, network aliases and Compose service names with the container's address on that network. Containers on different networks cannot resolve or reach each other, which isolates stacks.

blocks.text:
#### Publishing ports

A container address on a bridge network is private to the host. `-p HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT` (or `ports:` in Compose) makes a container port reachable through a host port. On a normal host Docker adds an iptables rule in the `nat` table: a DNAT rule rewrites the destination of packets arriving at the host port to the container address, and a MASQUERADE rule rewrites the source of outbound packets so that replies find their way back. A userland proxy process (`docker-proxy`) additionally handles connections that originate on the host itself.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Limits of the build machine. The daemon was started with `--iptables=false` and `--bridge=none`: no default `bridge` network exists, the `nat` table has no Docker rules (`iptables -t nat -S` showed only the default chains) and IPv4 forwarding is disabled (every container start prints `WARNING: IPv4 forwarding is disabled. Networking will not` `work.`). Container-to-container traffic on user-defined networks and host-to-published-port traffic through `docker-proxy` worked and are shown below. Traffic from outside the machine, from containers to the internet and NAT behaviour were not available and are described conceptually only.

### Worked example

Two small programs written for this guide are in the image `v2-base:1`: `srv PORT` listens and answers `hello from` `<hostname>`, and `cli HOST PORT` connects and prints the reply.

#### User-defined bridge and DNS

blocks.code:
$ docker network ls --format '{{.Name}}\t{{.Driver}}'
host    host
none    null
$ docker network create --driver bridge --subnet 172.30.0.0/24 v2-net
$ docker run -d --name v2-api --network v2-net --network-alias orders v2-base:1 srv 8080
$ docker network inspect v2-net --format '{{range .Containers}}{{.Name}} {{.IPv4Address}} {{end}}'
v2-api 172.30.0.2/24
$ docker run --rm --network v2-net v2-base:1 cli v2-api 8080
hello from 1f1db511f724
$ docker run --rm --network v2-net v2-base:1 cli orders 8080
hello from 1f1db511f724
$ docker run --rm --network v2-net v2-base:1 bash -c 'grep -E "nameserver|options" /etc/resolv.conf'
nameserver 127.0.0.11
options timeout:2 attempts:3 ndots:0
blocks.title: Name resolution on a user-defined network

blocks.text:
The client reached the server by container name and by network alias. The first output shows that no `bridge` network exists on this machine, which is a consequence of the daemon flags. The resolver address `127.0.0.11` is the embedded DNS server.

#### The localhost mistake and isolation

blocks.code:
$ docker run --rm --network v2-net v2-base:1 cli localhost 8080
connect: Connection refused
$ docker run --rm --network v2-net v2-base:1 cli nosuchhost 8080
resolve nosuchhost: Name or service not known
$ docker network create v2-net2
$ docker run --rm --network v2-net2 v2-base:1 cli v2-api 8080
resolve v2-api: Name or service not known
blocks.title: localhost is the container itself

blocks.text:
`localhost` in the client container refers to the client's own loopback interface, where nothing listens. The third command shows network isolation: from a different network the name does not resolve at all.

#### Sharing a network namespace

blocks.code:
$ docker run -d --name v2-main --network none v2-base:1 srv 8080
$ docker run --rm --network container:v2-main v2-base:1 cli localhost 8080
hello from 4e8eb5d9b1de
$ docker run --rm --network none v2-base:1 cli localhost 8080
connect: Connection refused
blocks.title: container:NAME joins the namespace

blocks.text:
A second container joined to the namespace of `v2-main` reaches the server on `localhost`; an unrelated container with its own empty namespace does not. This is how Kubernetes containers of one pod communicate.

#### Host mode and none

blocks.code:
$ docker run --rm --network none v2-base:1 bash -c 'cat /proc/net/dev | tail -n +3 | cut -d: -f1'
    lo
$ docker run -d --name v2-host --network host v2-base:1 srv 18081
$ ./cli localhost 18081                   # run on the host
hello from vm
$ docker run --rm --network host v2-base:1 \
    bash -c 'tail -n +3 /proc/net/dev | cut -d: -f1 | tr "\n" " "'
    lo   ifb0   ifb1   eth0
blocks.title: host and none

blocks.text:
In host mode the server bound port 18081 directly on the host (reply `vm` is the host name), and the container saw the host interfaces. Host mode has no isolation: two containers cannot bind the same port, and the container can reach services listening on the host's loopback.

#### Published port

blocks.code:
$ docker run -d --name v2-pub --network v2-pn -p 18082:8080 v2-base:1 srv 8080
$ docker port v2-pub
8080/tcp -> 0.0.0.0:18082
$ ./cli localhost 18082
hello from 7d5bfcfe9691
$ ps -eo pid,args | grep docker-proxy | grep -v grep
32337 /usr/bin/docker-proxy -proto tcp -host-ip 0.0.0.0 -host-port 18082 ...
$ iptables -t nat -S
-P PREROUTING ACCEPT
-P INPUT ACCEPT
-P OUTPUT ACCEPT
-P POSTROUTING ACCEPT
blocks.title: Port publishing on the build machine (userland proxy)

blocks.text:
The connection from the host succeeded through the `docker-proxy` process, while the NAT table stayed empty because iptables handling was disabled. On a standard installation the same command would add DNAT and MASQUERADE rules as shown conceptually in the figure above.

### Hands-on

Objective: build a two-container network and break it on purpose.

1. Create a user-defined network and start two containers on it, for example `docker run -d --name web --network` `lab nginx` and `docker run --rm --network lab curlimages/curl curl -s http://web` (any images with an HTTP server and client).
2. Resolve the name from the second container and note the IP returned (`docker network inspect lab`).
3. Replace the name with `localhost` and observe the failure.
4. Start a third container on a second network and confirm that it cannot resolve `web`; connect it to both networks with `docker network connect lab NAME` and retry.
5. Start the server with `-p 8081:80` and use `curl localhost:8081` from the host.

Expected result: name resolution works within one network only, `localhost` fails, `docker network connect` joins a container to an additional network and the published port answers on the host.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 16: connection refused to localhost inside a container

**Scenario.** `orders-service` is configured with `spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/orders`, which worked on the laptop, and is run in a container next to a `db` container.

**Symptoms.** Start-up fails with `Connection to localhost:5432 refused`. The database container is healthy and reachable from the host on its published port.

**Diagnosis.** From inside the application container, the experiment above (`cli localhost 8080`) fails in the same way. The demonstration application reports it in its health endpoint: with the default URL the response was `{"status":"DOWN","db":"unreachable localhost"}`.

**Root cause.** Every container has its own loopback interface. `localhost` inside the application container refers to that container, not to the host and not to the database container.

**Fix.** Use the service or container name on a shared user-defined network: `jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/orders`. Reach the host itself through `host.docker.internal` (available with Docker Desktop, and on Linux with `--add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway`, from memory) only when the dependency really runs on the host.

**Prevention.** Provide connection URLs through environment variables and test the container configuration, not the laptop configuration.

#### Problem 17: service reachable inside the network but not from the host

**Scenario.** `curl localhost:8080` from the host fails although the application is healthy.

**Symptoms.** `docker port NAME` prints nothing; `curl` reports connection refused.

**Diagnosis.** `docker ps` shows an empty PORTS column. If a port is published but still unreachable, check whether the application binds to `127.0.0.1` inside the container instead of `0.0.0.0`.

**Root cause.** Ports are published only with `-p` or `ports:` (the Dockerfile `EXPOSE` is documentation). A server bound to the container's loopback is not reachable through the bridge.

**Fix.** Publish the port and bind the server to `0.0.0.0` (Spring Boot does so by default; `server.address` must not be set to `127.0.0.1`).

**Prevention.** Include a published-port check in the smoke test of the Compose stack.

### Questions to expect

**Q1. How do containers find each other by name?** On a user-defined network the embedded DNS server at 127.0.0.11 resolves container names, aliases and Compose service names. The default bridge network offers no such resolution.

**Q2. Why does** `localhost` **fail between containers?** Each container has its own network namespace and loopback interface, so `localhost` is the container itself. Use the service name on a shared network.

**Q3. Explain** `-p 8080:80`**.** It maps host port 8080 to container port 80. Docker implements it with a DNAT rule (and a userland proxy for local connections), so traffic to the host's port 8080 is forwarded to the container's address.

**Q4. What is the difference between EXPOSE and publishing?** EXPOSE is metadata documenting a port. Publishing makes the port reachable from outside the container network.

**Q5. When is host networking appropriate?** When the container needs the host's network stack directly, for example monitoring agents or very high packet rates. It sacrifices isolation and port independence.

**Q6. How are two networks isolated and how can a container join both?** Containers on different bridge networks cannot reach each other. `docker network connect` attaches a running container to an additional network.

**Q7. What does** `--network container:NAME` **do?** The new container shares the other's network namespace, so both see the same interfaces and `localhost`.

**Q8. How does outbound traffic reach the internet from a container?** The container sends packets to the bridge gateway; the host forwards them (IP forwarding) and masquerades the source address with NAT. Not testable on the build machine.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Use user-defined networks: they provide DNS names and isolation; each stack gets its own network.
- localhost inside a container is the container; address other services by name.
- EXPOSE documents; -p or ports: publishes, by NAT rules (and docker-proxy for local connections).
- Host mode shares the host stack, none gives only loopback, container:NAME shares another container's namespace.
- State the limits of the environment: on the build machine NAT, forwarding and external traffic were unavailable, name resolution and local publishing worked.

An application such as `orders-service` consists of several containers: the service, a PostgreSQL database and, optionally, a cache. Starting them with separate `docker run` commands requires the reader to remember networks, volumes, environment variables and start order. **Docker Compose** describes the whole stack in one YAML file (`compose.yaml`) and starts, stops and inspects it with one command. Compose is used for local development, for integration tests in a pipeline and for small single-host deployments; production clusters use an orchestrator (see the Kubernetes chapters).

### Concept and mechanism

A Compose file follows the Compose Specification. The top-level keys are `services`, `networks`, `volumes`, `configs`, `secrets` and `name`. The obsolete `version:` key is not needed in current Compose (a warning is printed if it is present; from memory, verify against the current specification). The tool is invoked as `docker compose` (a plugin of the Docker CLI; version v5.5.1 on the build machine).

rows: Image to run; with `build` it is also the tag given to the built image
Build context (and Dockerfile, args, target) used by `docker compose build`
Environment variables inline or from files; `${VAR}` in the file is substituted from the shell or from `.env`
Networks the service joins; the service name becomes a DNS name
Start order; with `condition` the wait criterion
Same as the Dockerfile instruction, overriding it
Starts the service only when a profile is activated
blocks.caption: Important keys of a service.

blocks.text:
#### Start order and readiness

`depends_on` controls the order of creation and removal. By default it waits only until the dependency container is *running*. Per the Docker documentation (startup order page, consulted October 2026) the available conditions are `service_started`, `service_healthy` (the dependency's healthcheck must pass) and `service_completed_successfully` (the dependency must run to completion, suited to migration jobs). A running database is not yet a database that accepts connections, so applications that connect at start-up need `service_healthy`.

blocks.text:
#### Profiles, override files and variables

A service with `profiles: ["cache"]` is ignored unless `--profile cache` (or `COMPOSE_PROFILES`) is given. Compose reads `compose.yaml` and, when present, `compose.override.yaml` and merges them: maps are merged key by key, so the override file adds development settings (debug logging, extra ports, bind mounts) without touching the base file. More files can be combined with repeated `-f`. A `.env` file next to the compose file supplies values for `${VARIABLE}` substitution; `${VAR:?message}` makes the variable mandatory and `${VAR:-default}` supplies a default. Secrets must not be committed: `.env` belongs in `.gitignore` and in `.dockerignore`.

### Worked example

#### The compose.yaml for orders-service

The file below describes `orders-service`, PostgreSQL and an optional Redis cache. Image names are parameters so that the same file runs with locally built images (on the build machine the two variables point to the demonstration images; the real `postgres:16` and `redis:7` cannot be pulled there).

blocks.code:
name: orders

services:
  db:
    image: ${POSTGRES_IMAGE:-postgres:16}
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: orders_app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:?set DB_PASSWORD in .env}
      POSTGRES_DB: orders
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "pg_isready", "-U", "orders_app", "-d", "orders"]
      interval: 3s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10
    networks:
      - backend

  orders-service:
    image: ${ORDERS_IMAGE:-orders-service:dev}
    build:
      context: .
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    environment:
      SERVER_PORT: "8080"
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/orders
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME: orders_app
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "/app/healthcheck.sh"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 5s
    restart: unless-stopped
    networks:
      - backend

  redis:
    image: redis:7
    profiles: ["cache"]
    networks:
      - backend

volumes:
  pgdata:

networks:
  backend:

blocks.text:
#### Running the stack

The project name was set to `v2orders` with `-p` so that all objects carry the `v2` prefix.

blocks.code:
$ export POSTGRES_IMAGE=v2-postgres:16 ORDERS_IMAGE=v2-orders:1
$ docker compose -p v2orders config --services
db
orders-service
$ docker compose -p v2orders --profile cache config --services
db
orders-service
redis
blocks.title: docker compose config, profiles

blocks.code:
$ docker compose -p v2orders up -d --no-build --pull never
 Container v2orders-db-1 Started
 Container v2orders-db-1 Healthy
 Container v2orders-orders-service-1 Started
$ docker compose -p v2orders ps --format 'table {{.Service}}\t{{.Status}}'
SERVICE          STATUS
db               Up 18 seconds (healthy)
orders-service   Up 8 seconds (healthy)
$ curl -s localhost:8080/actuator/health
{"status":"UP"}
$ curl -s localhost:8080/orders
[{"id":1,"item":"book"}]
$ docker compose -p v2orders exec orders-service bash -c 'echo $SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL'
jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/orders
blocks.title: Start, inspect, call

blocks.text:
The application container started only after `Healthy` was reported for the database, and its own health status became `healthy` because the TCP check against `db:5432` succeeded. The host `curl` worked through the published port (the userland proxy, see the networking chapter).

#### Start order without the health condition

An override file (the `!override` tag is a Compose extension, so the listing is shown as plain text and is not parsed by standard YAML loaders) replaced the dependency with the short form (`depends_on: !override [db]`, which waits only for the container to run) and delayed the database by 8 seconds to imitate a slow start:

**compose.race.yaml**

blocks.code:
services:
  db:
    entrypoint: ["bash", "-c", "sleep 8; exec /usr/local/bin/entrypoint.sh"]
  orders-service:
    depends_on: !override
      - db

$ docker compose -p v2orders -f compose.yaml -f compose.race.yaml up -d --no-build --pull never
 Container v2orders-db-1 Started
 Container v2orders-orders-service-1 Started
$ sleep 4; ./probe.sh        # t+4 s
{"status":"DOWN","db":"unreachable db"}
$ sleep 10; ./probe.sh       # t+14 s
{"status":"UP"}
blocks.title: The race and its resolution

blocks.text:
Both containers started immediately, and the application reported `DOWN` while the database was initialising. The demonstration application polls the database on every health request and therefore recovers. A Spring Boot application that opens its connection pool at start-up would fail the start (typically with a `Connection refused` stack trace) and, with `restart: unless-stopped`, loop until the database is ready. With `service_healthy` the first Compose output above had no such window.

Persistence behaviour of `down` and `down -v` is covered with real output in the chapter on runtime and storage.

#### Compose for development and integration tests

For development, `compose.override.yaml` adds bind mounts of the source tree, a debug port and verbose logging without changing the base file. For integration tests in a pipeline, `docker compose up -d --wait` (waits for the services to be running or healthy; from memory, verify) starts the stack, tests run against `localhost:8080`, and `docker compose` `down -v` removes containers, network and volumes so that every run starts clean. In Java tests, **Testcontainers** starts the same kind of throwaway containers from test code (for example a `PostgreSQLContainer`); see the Spring Boot testing material. Compose suits end-to-end checks of the packaged image, Testcontainers suits tests that need a database inside the JVM test lifecycle.

### Hands-on

Objective: run the stack and observe start-order behaviour.

1. Create a directory with the `compose.yaml` above (use real images `postgres:16`, and for the application any image that exposes port 8080 and a `/actuator/health` endpoint, for example the image built in the Dockerfile chapter) and a `.env` file with `DB_PASSWORD=local-only`.
2. Run `docker compose config` and confirm that the variables were substituted.
3. Run `docker compose up -d`, then `docker compose ps` until both services are healthy.
4. Run `docker compose exec db psql -U orders_app -d orders -c 'select 1'`.
5. Replace the dependency condition by the short form `depends_on: [db]`, run `docker compose down` and `up -d`, and observe whether the application logs connection errors during start-up.
6. Remove everything with `docker compose down -v`.

Expected result: substituted values in step 2, both services healthy in step 3, and (depending on database speed) connection errors in step 5 that disappear with `service_healthy`.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 18: the application starts before the database is ready

**Scenario.** After `docker compose up` the `orders-service` container exits or reports errors while the database is still initialising.

**Symptoms.** `Connection refused` or `the database system is starting up` in the application log, followed by restarts.

**Diagnosis.** `docker compose ps` shows the database `starting` (not `healthy`) when the application starts. The experiment above reproduced it: the health endpoint returned `{"status":"DOWN","db":"unreachable db"}` at 4 seconds.

**Root cause.** `depends_on` without a condition waits only for the container to run. A database process that is running is not yet accepting connections.

**Fix.** Add a `healthcheck` to the database (`pg_isready`) and `depends_on: db: condition: service_healthy`. In addition, configure connection retries in the application (HikariCP `initializationFailTimeout`, Spring Retry) so that the service survives a database restart later.

**Prevention.** Treat start order as a readiness problem rather than a sequencing problem, in Compose and in Kubernetes alike.

#### Problem 19: every developer has a different configuration

**Scenario.** The stack works for one developer and fails for another with `variable is not set` or wrong ports.

**Symptoms.** A warning that `DB_PASSWORD` is not set, or a port conflict on 8080.

**Diagnosis.** `docker compose config` prints the effective, substituted file and shows which values were used and which files were merged.

**Root cause.** Environment-specific values were taken from the developer's shell or from an untracked `.env` that differs between machines.

**Fix.** Commit an `.env.example` with names and harmless defaults, use `${VAR:?message}` for mandatory values and `${VAR:-default}` for optional ones, and keep personal changes in `compose.override.yaml`.

**Prevention.** Run `docker compose config` in the pipeline to detect unresolved variables.

### Questions to expect

**Q1. What problem does Docker Compose solve?** It defines a multi-container application (services, networks, volumes, configuration) in one file and manages it with single commands, making local and test environments reproducible.

**Q2. How do services find each other in Compose?** Compose creates a user-defined network and registers each service name in the embedded DNS, so `jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/orders` resolves.

**Q3. What does** `depends_on` **guarantee?** Start (and stop) order. By default only that the dependency container is running. With `condition: service_healthy` the dependency must also pass its healthcheck; `service_completed_successfully` waits for a job to finish.

**Q4. What are profiles?** A way to mark optional services (for example a cache or debugging tools) that start only when the profile is activated.

**Q5. How are environment-specific values supplied?** Through `environment`, `env_file`, `${VAR}` substitution from the shell or `.env`, and override files.

**Q6. What is** `compose.override.yaml`**?** A file merged automatically over `compose.yaml`, used for development settings. Other combinations are chosen with `-f`.

**Q7. What is the difference between** `down` **and** `down -v`**?** `down` removes containers and networks but keeps named volumes; `-v` also removes the volumes and therefore the data.

**Q8. Compose or Testcontainers for integration tests?** Compose starts the packaged stack from outside the code and suits end-to-end tests; Testcontainers starts containers from test code and suits tests inside the build.

**Q9. Is Compose suitable for production?** Acceptable for a single host with modest availability needs; it lacks multi-host scheduling, rolling updates and self-healing across nodes, which orchestrators provide.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- One compose.yaml describes services, networks and volumes; services reach each other by service name.
- Use healthchecks with depends\_on condition service\_healthy; plain depends\_on only orders container start.
- Keep secrets out of the file: variables with ${VAR:?}, an untracked .env, override files for local changes.
- docker compose config shows the effective result; down keeps volumes, down -v deletes them.
- Compose suits development, integration tests and single-host setups.

An image built on a laptop or a pipeline runner must reach the servers that run it. A **registry** is a service that stores images in repositories and serves them over the HTTP API of the OCI Distribution Specification. Pushing and pulling are the delivery mechanism of container-based systems, so the way images are named and tagged determines whether a deployment can be traced, repeated and rolled back.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Naming

An image reference has the form `REGISTRY/NAMESPACE/REPOSITORY:TAG@DIGEST`. A missing registry means Docker Hub, a missing tag means `latest`. The tag and the digest are optional; when both are present the digest decides.

#### Tagging strategy

Tags are mutable, so a strategy is needed:

- **Immutable build tags**: tag every build with the git commit SHA (`orders-service:git-3f9c2a1`). The tag identifies the exact source and is never reassigned.
- **Semantic version tags**: `1.4.2` for releases, optionally also `1.4` and `1`. Release tags are created once from the tested image.
- **Environment pointers**: `staging` or `prod` tags that move are convenient but untraceable; deployment manifests should reference the immutable tag or digest.
- `latest`: only a default for `docker pull` without a tag. It does not mean newest, it is moved by whoever pushes it, and it makes rollbacks and audits impossible. Do not deploy it.

**Digest pinning** references `orders-service@sha256:...` and guarantees the bytes. It is the strongest protection against a tag being re-pointed (accidentally or maliciously), at the cost of readability; deployment tooling that records the digest of the tested image provides both.

#### Integrity and scanning

Digest verification proves that the content equals what was addressed. **Image signing** (for example Sigstore `cosign`, covered with supply-chain security later) proves who produced the image. **Vulnerability scanning** compares the packages and libraries in the layers against vulnerability databases; a scanner such as Trivy runs in the pipeline and fails the build above a severity threshold. Scanning and signing were not run on the build machine, which has no network access.

### Worked example

A registry cannot be reached from the build machine, so the same workflow was performed with `docker save` and `docker load`, which transport an image as a tar archive (also the method for air-gapped hosts).

blocks.code:
$ docker tag v2-cache:1 v2-cache:git-3f9c2a1
$ docker images v2-cache --format '{{.Repository}}:{{.Tag}} {{.ID}}'
v2-cache:1 aa9547b2f08c
v2-cache:git-3f9c2a1 aa9547b2f08c
$ docker save v2-cache:git-3f9c2a1 -o c.tar; ls -l c.tar | awk '{print $5}'
360960
$ docker rmi v2-cache:git-3f9c2a1 v2-cache:1
$ docker images v2-cache -q | wc -l
0
$ docker load -i c.tar
Loaded image: v2-cache:git-3f9c2a1
$ docker run --rm v2-cache:git-3f9c2a1
svc=orders version=22

A real push needs authentication and a repository path. These commands are illustrative (not run):

echo "$GHCR_TOKEN" | docker login ghcr.io -u ram --password-stdin

`--password-stdin` keeps the token out of the process list and shell history. The registry host and user are examples; the GitHub Actions workflow that does this automatically is covered in the continuous delivery material.

### Hands-on

Objective: practise tagging and archive transport.

1. Tag an image three ways: `docker tag app:dev app:1.0.0`, `docker tag app:dev app:git-SHORTSHA`, `docker tag` `app:dev app:latest`.
2. List them with `docker images` and confirm the identical image ID.
3. Export one tag with `docker save -o app.tar app:1.0.0`, remove all tags with `docker rmi`, and import with `docker load -i app.tar`.
4. If a registry is available (a local one can be started with the open-source `registry:2` image), push, delete the local copy, pull by digest and compare `docker image inspect --format '{{.RepoDigests}}'`.

Expected result: one image ID for all tags and identical behaviour after load.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 20: production runs a different version than expected

**Scenario.** A hotfix was pushed as `orders-service:latest`, but one node still serves old behaviour.

**Symptoms.** Two nodes answer differently; `docker ps` shows the same tag on both.

**Diagnosis.** Compare the image IDs or digests with `docker image inspect --format '{{.Id}}'` (or `{{.RepoDigests}}`) on each node. The nodes pulled `latest` at different times, or one never pulled again because the tag existed locally.

**Root cause.** `latest` is a mutable tag, and `docker run` does not re-pull an image that is present locally.

**Fix.** Deploy immutable tags (commit SHA or version) or digests and pull explicitly (`docker pull`, `--pull always`, Compose `pull_policy: always`).

**Prevention.** Forbid `latest` in deployment files and record the digest of every released image.

#### Problem 21: pull fails with unauthorized or denied

**Scenario.** A server cannot pull a private image.

**Symptoms.** `pull access denied` or `unauthorized: authentication required`.

**Diagnosis.** Check `docker login` state (`~/.docker/config.json` holds credentials or a credential helper) and the repository path and spelling; private repositories appear as non-existent to unauthenticated clients.

**Root cause.** Missing or expired credentials, token without the read-package scope, or a wrong registry host.

**Fix.** Log in with a token that has pull permission (a read-only deploy token or an IAM role for ECR) and verify the image name.

**Prevention.** Use short-lived or read-only credentials for servers, never personal tokens, and rotate them.

### Questions to expect

**Q1. What is a registry and what is a repository?** A registry is the service storing images; a repository inside it holds the versions (tags) of one image name.

**Q2. Why avoid** `latest` **in production?** It is mutable and ambiguous: different hosts may hold different images and rollbacks cannot be named. Use immutable version or commit tags.

**Q3. What is the benefit of pinning by digest?** The digest is a hash of the manifest, so the pulled bytes are exactly the tested bytes even if a tag is re-pointed.

**Q4. Which tags should a release build produce?** A commit-SHA tag for every build, and semantic version tags created when the build is promoted to a release.

**Q5. How can an image be transferred without a registry?** `docker save` writes a tar archive and `docker load` reads it, which is useful for air-gapped systems and for caching in pipelines.

**Q6. What is image signing for?** It proves provenance (who built the image) in addition to integrity, so that deployment policies can reject unsigned images.

**Q7. What does a vulnerability scanner inspect?** The operating-system packages and application dependencies found in the image layers, compared with vulnerability databases. It reports known issues; it does not find unknown flaws.

**Q8. How are credentials for pushing handled in CI?** By a token stored in the CI secret store and passed with `docker login --password-stdin`, or by short-lived identity federation instead of long-lived keys.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A reference is registry/namespace/repository:tag@digest; tags move, digests do not.
- Tag every build with the commit SHA, release with semantic versions, and never deploy latest.
- Pin digests where reproducibility matters; add signing and scanning to the pipeline.
- docker save and docker load move images without a registry.
- Use least-privilege, short-lived credentials for pulling and pushing.

A container shares the host kernel, runs as root by default and contains whatever the image builder put into its layers. Three kinds of weakness follow: secrets baked into layers that anyone with the image can read, containers that grant an attacker more power than the application needs, and access to the Docker daemon, which is equivalent to root on the host. This chapter demonstrates each with commands and lists the controls that reduce the risk.

blocks.text:
#### Principles

- **Least privilege.** Run as a non-root numeric user, drop all Linux capabilities and add back only what is required, set `no-new-privileges`, use a read-only root file system with explicit writable tmpfs or volumes, and set memory and process limits.
- **Minimal image.** Fewer packages mean fewer vulnerabilities and fewer tools for an intruder. Prefer slim or distroless runtime bases, multi-stage builds and pinned versions; rebuild regularly.
- **No secrets in images.** Anything written to a layer, an `ARG` or an `ENV` is retained and extractable. Pass secrets at run time (secret stores, mounted files) and use BuildKit secret mounts for build-time credentials.
- **Protect the daemon.** The Docker socket gives complete control; never mount it into a container unless that container is trusted as root on the host.
- **Isolation of workloads.** User-defined networks per stack, resource limits, seccomp and AppArmor profiles (defaults are applied by Docker; the build machine reports `name=seccomp,profile=builtin`) and, for strong tenant isolation, virtual machines or sandboxed runtimes.
- **Rootless mode.** The daemon and containers can run as an unprivileged user through user namespaces, so a container escape yields an unprivileged host user. It has restrictions (privileged ports, some networking and storage options); it was not tested on the build machine.

### Worked example

#### A secret in a layer

A Dockerfile copies a file with a password, deletes it in the next instruction and takes a token as a build argument:

blocks.code:
FROM v2-base:1
ARG API_TOKEN
COPY secrets.env /tmp/secrets.env
RUN echo "token length: ${#API_TOKEN}" && rm /tmp/secrets.env
CMD ["ls", "/tmp"]
blocks.title: Dockerfile.bad

blocks.text: The image was built with `--build-arg API_TOKEN=ghp_FAKE0123456789` (a made-up value). The running container shows no secret (`ls /tmp` prints nothing), yet:

blocks.code:
$ docker history --no-trunc --format '{{.CreatedBy}}' v2-leaky:1 | head -4
CMD ["ls" "/tmp"]
RUN |1 API_TOKEN=ghp_FAKE0123456789 /bin/sh -c echo "token length: ${#API_TOKEN}" \
  && rm /tmp/secrets.env # buildkit
COPY secrets.env /tmp/secrets.env # buildkit
ARG API_TOKEN=ghp_FAKE0123456789
blocks.title: History reveals the argument

blocks.code:
$ docker save v2-leaky:1 -o i.tar && mkdir x && tar -C x -xf i.tar
$ for l in $(layers listed in x/manifest.json); do tar tf x/$l | grep secrets; done
tmp/secrets.env
tmp/.wh.secrets.env
$ tar xOf x/blobs/sha256/a62e4b6d... tmp/secrets.env
DB_PASSWORD=hunter2-not-a-real-password
blocks.title: The deleted file is still in an earlier layer

blocks.text:
One layer contains `tmp/secrets.env` with its content; the next layer contains only the whiteout `tmp/.wh.secrets.env`. The build argument is recorded in the image configuration (a scan of the decompressed blobs found the token in the config JSON). Anyone who can pull the image can read both.

The remedy for build-time credentials is a BuildKit secret mount, which exposes the secret to one `RUN` at `/run/secrets/ID` without storing it:

blocks.code:
FROM v2-base:1
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=api_token \
    echo "token length: $(wc -c < /run/secrets/api_token)" > /tmp/build-info.txt
CMD ["cat", "/tmp/build-info.txt"]
blocks.title: Dockerfile.good

blocks.code:
$ docker build --secret id=api_token,src=token.txt -t v2-clean:1 -f Dockerfile.good .
$ docker run --rm v2-clean:1
token length: 18
$ docker history --no-trunc --format '{{.CreatedBy}}' v2-clean:1 | head -2
CMD ["cat" "/tmp/build-info.txt"]
RUN /bin/sh -c echo "token length: $(wc -c < /run/secrets/api_token)" \
  > /tmp/build-info.txt # buildkit
$ for f in x/blobs/sha256/*; do zcat -f $f | grep -aq ghp_FAKE && echo "FOUND in $f"; done
$ echo "scan finished, nothing found"
scan finished, nothing found
blocks.title: Build with a secret mount and scan every layer

blocks.text:
The token (18 bytes) was usable during the build, and a scan of every decompressed blob of the saved image found it nowhere. In multi-stage builds a secret copied in a builder stage does not reach the final image, because only explicitly copied files are included; this is a second protection but does not replace the secret mount, because the builder stage remains in the build cache.

#### Running with least privilege

blocks.code:
$ docker run --rm v2-base:1 bash -c 'id -u; grep CapEff /proc/self/status'
0
CapEff: 00000000a80425fb
$ docker run --rm --read-only --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges \
    --user 10001:10001 --tmpfs /tmp:rw,mode=1777,size=16m v2-base:1 \
    bash -c 'touch /etc/probe; touch /tmp/ok && echo "/tmp is writable"'
touch: cannot touch '/etc/probe': Read-only file system
/tmp is writable
$ docker run --rm --cap-drop CHOWN v2-base:1 bash -c 'touch /tmp/f; chown 1:1 /tmp/f'
chown: changing ownership of '/tmp/f': Operation not permitted
blocks.title: Default container compared with a hardened one

blocks.text:
The default container runs as UID 0 with a set of capabilities (effective mask `a80425fb`, a reduced set compared with full root). The hardened run executed as UID 10001, could not write the root file system and wrote only to the declared tmpfs; it also had an empty capability set and `NoNewPrivs` set (the `grep` of `CapEff` printed `0000000000000000` and `NoNewPrivs: 1` in the underlying experiment). Even root lost a single permission when one capability was dropped. A tmpfs mounted without `mode=1777` is root-owned with mode 755 in this image because the base `/tmp` directory has mode 755; images built from standard distributions have a world-writable `/tmp`.

#### The Docker socket

A container started with the daemon socket mounted can control the daemon:

blocks.code:
$ docker run -d --name v2-sock -v /tmp/dk/d.sock:/var/run/docker.sock v2-tools:1 sleep 60
$ docker exec v2-sock env DOCKER_HOST=unix:///var/run/docker.sock docker ps --format '{{.Names}}'
v2-sock
$ docker exec v2-sock env DOCKER_HOST=unix:///var/run/docker.sock \
    docker run --rm -v /etc:/host-etc:ro v2-base:1 bash -c 'head -1 /host-etc/hostname'
vm
blocks.title: Socket mounted into a container (private daemon)

blocks.text:
From inside the container, a new container was started that mounted the host's `/etc` and read the host name; with a writable mount of `/` the same method can modify any host file. Mounting the socket therefore grants root on the host. The same applies to membership of the `docker` group. CI jobs that build images should use rootless builders or daemonless tools rather than the host's socket.

### Hands-on

Objective: find a secret in an image and harden a container.

1. Write a Dockerfile that copies a file `secret.txt` and removes it in a later `RUN`. Build it.
2. Search for the secret with `docker save IMAGE | tar -xO` per layer, or with `docker save IMAGE -o i.tar`, extraction and `grep` over the decompressed layers.
3. Rebuild with `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=s ...` and `docker build --secret id=s,src=secret.txt .`, then repeat the search.
4. Run any image with `--read-only --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges --user 10001:10001` and note which operations fail; add `--tmpfs /tmp` where the application needs writable space.
5. If a scanner such as Trivy is installed, scan the image and read the severity summary.

Expected result: the secret is found in step 2 and absent in step 3; the hardened run reveals every place where the application assumed root.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 22: a credential is found in a published image

**Scenario.** A security review pulls the public image of the service.

**Symptoms.** The password of a database user appears in `docker history` output or in an extracted layer.

**Diagnosis.** `docker history --no-trunc` exposes `ARG` values and commands; layer extraction (as above) exposes deleted files.

**Root cause.** Secrets passed by `ARG`/`ENV` or copied and later deleted stay in the image because layers are additive.

**Fix.** Revoke and rotate the credential immediately (the image must be treated as compromised, deleting the tag is not sufficient because copies exist), rebuild without the secret and publish a new image.

**Prevention.** Use BuildKit secret mounts and runtime secret injection, scan images and repositories for secrets in the pipeline, and keep `.env` and key files in `.dockerignore`.

#### Problem 23: application fails after switching to a hardened configuration

**Scenario.** `--read-only` and a non-root user are enabled and the service stops working.

**Symptoms.** `Read-only file system` or `Permission denied` on start-up, for temp files, caches or logs.

**Diagnosis.** The log shows the path; `docker diff NAME` lists files the container tried to write on a normal run, which identifies the directories that need to be writable.

**Root cause.** The application writes to places that were writable only because it ran as root with a writable root file system (for example `/tmp`, a work directory, a log directory).

**Fix.** Mount tmpfs or volumes on exactly those paths (`--tmpfs /tmp`, `-v work:/work`), set `java.io.tmpdir` if needed and make directories writable for the numeric user.

**Prevention.** Develop and test with the hardened flags from the start (in Compose: `read_only: true`, `cap_drop:` `[ALL]`, `user: "10001"`).

### Questions to expect

**Q1. Why is running as root in a container a risk?** UID 0 in the container is UID 0 on the host unless user namespaces are used. A container escape or a mounted host path then gives root access. A non-root numeric user limits the damage.

**Q2. How can a secret end up in an image, and how is it avoided?** Through `ARG`, `ENV` or files copied into a layer; deleting the file later does not remove it. Use BuildKit secret mounts at build time and runtime secret injection.

**Q3. What do** `--read-only`**,** `--cap-drop ALL` **and** `no-new-privileges` **do?** A read-only root file system prevents modification of the image content; dropping capabilities removes kernel privileges such as chown or raw sockets; `no-new-privileges` stops setuid binaries from gaining privileges.

**Q4. Why is mounting the Docker socket dangerous?** It allows creating privileged containers or containers that mount the host file system, which is root on the host.

**Q5. What is a minimal or distroless image?** An image containing the application and its runtime libraries but no shell or package manager, which reduces vulnerabilities and tools available to an attacker, at the cost of harder debugging.

**Q6. What is rootless mode?** The daemon and containers run as an unprivileged user using user namespaces, so root in the container maps to an ordinary host user.

**Q7. How do vulnerability scanners work and what are their limits?** They match installed package and library versions against vulnerability databases. They report known issues, produce false positives and negatives and do not find unknown flaws.

**Q8. Why pin base image versions or digests and still rebuild regularly?** Pinning makes builds reproducible; regular rebuilds pick up security patches of the base image. Automation (a dependency bot) proposes updated pins.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Secrets in ARG, ENV or deleted files remain in the layers; docker history and layer extraction reveal them. Use BuildKit secret mounts.
- Run as a numeric non-root user with a read-only root file system, no capabilities, no-new-privileges and resource limits.
- Mounting docker.sock or joining the docker group equals root on the host.
- Prefer minimal base images, multi-stage builds, pinned versions, scanning and signing.
- A leaked secret must be revoked and rotated; deleting the image is not enough.

Containers fail in a small number of recognisable ways: the process exits, it is killed, it never becomes healthy, it cannot be reached or it behaves differently from the laptop. Each failure leaves evidence in the exit code, the logs, the container state and the namespaces. A fixed sequence of commands finds the cause faster than guesswork.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Exit codes

The exit code of a container is the exit status of its main process. Values above 128 mean termination by signal number minus 128.

rows: A shell without a terminal, a one-shot command
Permission denied on the program file
Wrong ENTRYPOINT or CMD, missing program in the image
Out-of-memory kill, or `docker stop` timeout expired
Normal stop of a program that handles SIGTERM

blocks.text:
### Worked example

#### Reproducing the exit codes

blocks.code:
$ docker run --rm v2-base:1 bash -c 'exit 0'; echo $?
0
$ docker run --rm v2-base:1 bash -c 'echo failing; exit 1'; echo $?
failing
1
$ docker run --rm v2-base:1 nosuchcmd; echo $?
docker: Error response from daemon: ... exec: "nosuchcmd": executable file not found in $PATH
127
$ docker run --rm v2-base:1 /etc/passwd; echo $?
docker: Error response from daemon: ... exec: "/etc/passwd": permission denied
126
$ docker run --rm --nosuchflag v2-base:1; echo $?
unknown flag: --nosuchflag
125
blocks.title: Exit codes 0, 1, 125, 126, 127

blocks.text:
Exit 137 and 143 were produced earlier: `docker kill` and a `docker stop` of a process without a SIGTERM handler gave 137 (container `sleep` as PID 1), a Java process with a shutdown hook gave 143, and an OOM kill gave 137 with `OOMKilled=true`.

#### Inspecting a running container

blocks.code:
$ docker run -d --name v2-tr v2-base:1 sleep 100; sleep 1; docker stop -t 1 v2-tr; docker rm v2-tr
$ docker events --since $START --until $END --filter container=v2-tr \
    --format '{{.Type}} {{.Action}}'
container create
container start
container kill
container kill
container stop
container die
container destroy
blocks.title: docker events for one container lifecycle

blocks.code:
$ docker top v2-tr -o pid,user,args
PID                 USER                COMMAND
32619               10001               java -jar /app/orders-lite.jar
$ docker stats --no-stream --format 'table {{.Name}}\t{{.CPUPerc}}\t{{.MemUsage}}\t{{.PIDs}}' v2-tr
NAME      CPU %     MEM USAGE / LIMIT   PIDS
v2-tr     0.19%     20.41MiB / 128MiB   15
$ docker inspect v2-tr \
    --format 'State={{.State.Status}} Pid={{.State.Pid}} Health={{.State.Health.Status}}'
State=running Pid=32619 Health=starting
blocks.title: top, stats and inspect

blocks.text:
The `docker top` output lists the process with its host PID (32619, as in `State.Pid`), which links the container to the host tools.

#### nsenter: host tools inside container namespaces

When an image has no shell or tools (distroless images), the host's tools can be run inside the container's namespaces with `nsenter`:

blocks.code:
$ nsenter --target 32619 --pid --mount ps -e -o pid,comm
    PID COMMAND
      1 java
     21 ps
$ nsenter --target 32619 --net cat /proc/net/dev | tail -n +3 | cut -d: -f1
    lo
blocks.title: nsenter (as root on the host)

blocks.text:
The first command ran the host's `ps` inside the PID and mount namespaces of the container; the second read the network interfaces of the container's network namespace (only `lo`, because the container ran with `--network none`). Use `--net` with host tools such as `ss` to inspect sockets of a container whose image contains no networking tools.

### Hands-on

Objective: diagnose three prepared failures.

1. Run `docker run -d --name f1 IMAGE bash` (shell without a terminal), then use `docker ps -a` and `docker inspect` `-f '{{.State.ExitCode}}' f1`.
2. Run `docker run -d --name f2 --memory 64m IMAGE sh -c 'tail /dev/zero'` (allocates memory until killed) and read the exit code and `OOMKilled`.
3. Run `docker run -d --name f3 --health-cmd false --health-interval 1s IMAGE sleep 60`, wait five seconds and read `docker inspect -f '{{json .State.Health}}' f3`.
4. Start a server container on a user-defined network and from a client container reach it by `localhost` and then by name.
5. Remove all containers created in the exercise with `docker rm -f f1 f2 f3`.

Expected result: exit code 0, exit code 137 with `OOMKilled=true`, health `unhealthy` with a failing streak, and a connection refused for `localhost` against a success by name.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 24: container restarts in a loop (CrashLoop)

**Scenario.** A service with `restart: unless-stopped` starts, runs briefly and restarts repeatedly.

**Symptoms.** `docker ps` shows `Restarting (1) 5 seconds ago`; the restart count rises (in the experiment a one-second failing process reached 4 restarts within seven seconds).

**Diagnosis.** `docker logs --tail 100 NAME` (logs survive restarts), `docker inspect -f '{{.State.ExitCode}}` `{{.State.Error}}' NAME` and the exit code table.

**Root cause.** The main process fails at start-up: missing environment variable, unreachable dependency, wrong command (127) or permission problem (126).

**Fix.** Correct the configuration. To inspect the environment, start a shell with the same image and settings: `docker run` `--rm -it --entrypoint sh IMAGE`. **Prevention.** Fail fast with a clear message on missing configuration, add readiness-aware start order and alert on restart counts.

#### Problem 25: the image runs on the laptop but fails on the server

**Scenario.** The container exits immediately on the server with `exec format error`.

**Symptoms.** `standard_init_linux.go: exec user process caused: exec format error`, or a platform warning.

**Diagnosis.** Compare `docker image inspect --format '{{.Architecture}}'` with `uname -m` on the server.

**Root cause.** The image was built for another CPU architecture (for example arm64 on a Mac, amd64 on the server).

**Fix.** Build for the target platform (`docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64`) or publish a multi-platform image through an image index.

**Prevention.** Build release images in CI on the target architecture or explicitly with `--platform`.

### Questions to expect

**Q1. What does exit code 137 mean?** The process was killed by SIGKILL (128 + 9), usually by the kernel OOM killer (`OOMKilled=true`) or by `docker stop` after the timeout.

**Q2. What do 126 and 127 mean?** 126: the command exists but cannot be executed (permissions or format). 127: the command was not found in the image.

**Q3. A container is** `Exited (0)` **a second after start. Why?** Its main process finished, for example an interactive shell without a terminal or a daemon that forked into the background.

**Q4. How are the logs of a crashed container read?** `docker logs NAME` works for stopped containers as long as they are not removed (and the logging driver supports reading).

**Q5. How is a container with no shell debugged?** From the host with `nsenter -t PID` using host tools, with `docker` `cp`, or with an ephemeral debug container sharing its namespaces (`--pid container:NAME --network` `container:NAME`).

**Q6. What do** `docker top`**,** `docker stats` **and** `docker events` **show?** Processes of one container with host PIDs, live CPU, memory, I/O and PIDs per container, and the stream of daemon events such as create, start, kill, die, destroy.

**Q7. How is an unhealthy container investigated?** `docker inspect` shows the last health check outputs; run the same command manually with `docker exec`, and verify the command exists in the image and the start period is long enough.

**Q8. What does** `exec format error` **indicate?** An architecture mismatch between image and host, or a script without an interpreter line.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Read the exit code first: 0 normal, 1 to 2 application, 125 to 127 invocation, 137 SIGKILL or OOM, 143 SIGTERM.
- Use docker logs, inspect, events, stats and top before entering the container.
- nsenter runs host tools inside container namespaces, which helps with minimal images.
- Most connectivity faults are localhost misuse, missing publishing or different networks.
- Always confirm architecture, health command presence and start-period for containers that restart or never become healthy.
